newsitem.title: USA: CIGNA gains power, new markets with deal.
newsitem.headline: CIGNA gains power, new markets with deal.

text.p: CIGNA Corp's proposed $1.7 billion acquisition of Healthsource Inc gives its greater bargaining power in the intensely competitive health insurance business as well as a significant new presence in several key markets.
CIGNA also solidified its position as a health insurance consolidator and is likely to pursue additional deals, analysts said.
"They've laid the groundwork for a stronger healthcare operation with this transaction," A.M. Best senior vice president Larry Mayewski said.
But, this is not likely to be CIGNA's last health insurance deal, analysts said.

"I don't think this will be the end of things," said Mark Puccia, director of Standard & Poor's insurance rating services. "CIGNA is committed to the managed care marketplace," he said, and will continue to act as a consolidator.
The deal comes nearly one year after Aetna Inc agreed to buy U.S. Healthcare for $8.9 billion in a move that put its healthcare rivals on competitive notice.
"There's no doubt that when Aetna bought U.S. Healthcare, they raised the competitive hurdles," Mayewski said.
CIGNA's agreement to buy Healthsource now puts renewed pressure on Prudential Insurance Co of America, he said.
"Prudential has made no secret about the fact that they will be reassessing what it takes to compete in the healthcare business," Mayewski said.
And that evaluation process, he said, is still underway.
"It surely makes the marketplace more difficult and competitive for them" Mayewski said. "And that will obviously play an important role in their decision making," he said.
The Aetna and CIGNA deals also reflect the the effort by the traditional multi-line insurers to reshape their businesses to focus on growth markets.
CIGNA's domestic property-casualty operations, once about 40 percent of its overall business, now represent less than 10 percent, Sanford C. Bernstein analyst Weston Hicks said.

"The company is changing and becoming predominantly a global accident, life and health and pension company with a small specialized property-casualty business, which they may or may not keep," he said.
"It's not the same company it used to be," he said.
But with the Healthsource deal, CIGNA significantly closes the gap on market leader Aetna, giving it just under 12 million covered lives compared to Aetna's 14 million.
CIGNA gains a new presence in Maine, New Hampshire, South Carolina and Arkansas and a meaningful boost in membership in Tennessee, North Carolina and Massachusetts.
"It fills in some gaps," Standard & Poor's Puccia said.

With the deal, "they've gained additional scale, they surely, potentially will achieve some cost reductions, they may have enhanced their negotiation clout with providers to a certain extent," he said.

"But like anything, they will have to execute in terms of ultimately delivering on the financial ends of this transaction," Mayewski said. And it is still too early to know if that will happen, he said.
Indeed, Puccia said Standard & Poor's is concerned about the deal's impact on CIGNA's financial structure.

S&P said it may cut some of CIGNA's debt ratings. A.M. Best said it put CIGNA's life insurance rating under review and Duff & Phelps said it put CIGNA's debt and commercial paper ratings under review.
S&P's Puccia said he was concerned about the increase in CIGNA's debt and the additional strain the deal will put on the capitalization of CIGNA's operating companies.
CIGNA agreed to assume $250 million of Healthsource's outstanding long-term debt as part of the deal.
In addition, CIGNA has said it plans to pay for the acquisition by borrowing $650 million in the long-term markets.
